sentences.show: The Gestapo called her the White Mouse. Every time they closed in, she slipped away.
Her name was Nancy Wake, a girl from New Zealand, married to a rich Frenchman in Marseille.
When Germany took France in 1940, she began smuggling Allied airmen out to Spain.
She flirted her way past German checkpoints. In her words: "Do you want to search me?"
By 1943, the Gestapo was tapping her phone. She fled over the Pyrenees.
Her husband stayed behind. The Gestapo tortured him, and killed him. She didn't find out until the war was over.
In Britain, she trained as a secret agent. In April 1944, she parachuted back into France.
She landed tangled in a tree.
Then she ran the money and weapons for the Resistance, dropped by plane almost every other night.
She said she once cycled 500 kilometres in three days, to reach a radio.
And she said she killed an SS sentry with her bare hands.
Some of it only comes from her own memoir. But the medals are real.
Britain, America and France all decorated her.
When Australia offered medals decades later, she told them where they could stick them.
Nancy Wake died in 2011, aged 98. Her ashes were scattered in the French hills where she fought.
The Gestapo never caught her. Don't let her story slip away. Subscribe.
